analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement of equal pay for women, adding damages, wage transparency, and data collection.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 193 cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it easier for women to win pay discrimination cases against their employers. It tightens the legal defenses employers can use, lets workers recover compensatory and punitive damages, protects employees from retaliation for discussing their wages, bans contracts that forbid wage disclosure, and allows pay discrimination cases to proceed as class actions. It would also require employers to report pay and hiring data broken down by sex and race so regulators can spot discrimination patterns.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are underpaid relative to male colleagues doing equal work gain a realistic path to recover lost wages, plus compensatory damages (and punitive damages when employers act with malice). All workers gain from stronger protections against retaliation for asking about or disclosing pay, and the ban on wage-confidentiality clauses [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Narrows the employer defenses to paying different wages to men and women for the same work, requiring any pay gap to rest on a job-related, business-necessary factor that accounts for the entire gap [S2][S3].
Adds compensatory damages and, where an employer showed malice or reckless indifference, punitive damages — remedies the Equal Pay Act currently lacks [S3].
Protects workers from retaliation for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, and makes it illegal to require employees to sign contracts barring wage disclosure [S2][S3].
Allows pay discrimination claims to be brought as class actions without individual written consent, and lets the Labor Secretary seek damages on workers' behalf [S2][S3].

Requires the EEOC to issue rules collecting compensation, hiring, firing, and promotion data from employers broken down by sex, race, and national origin, to give enforcers the evidence to detect patterns of discrimination [S2][S3].
Authorizes $15 million for wage-discrimination enforcement training and negotiation-skills grants for girls and women, with exemptions and compliance materials for small businesses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers found to have sex-based pay gaps would owe back pay plus compensatory and potentially punitive damages, and face class actions and new federal reporting of compensation and employment data by sex, race, and national origin [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers and business groups have argued the stricter legal standard would invite costly litigation and force compliance costs on companies, including those paying different wages for legitimate reasons they would now have to prove in court [S3].

The mandatory collection of pay data disaggregated by sex and race would impose new reporting burdens on employers, though the bill directs the EEOC to weigh those burdens when writing the rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — enforceable equal pay with real damages, wage transparency, and data to prove discrimination — fall on employers who are paying women less for equal work. Employers with no pay gap keep every legitimate defense, and small businesses keep their Fair Labor Standards Act exemptions, so the main cost falls on those engaged in the discrimination the law already prohibits but does little to punish.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its subcommittees, and the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act in the House on March 25, 2015 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, and in November 2015 to two of its subcommittees [S5].
The bill attracted 193 cosponsors, 192 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote on the bill appears in its action history for the remainder of the 114th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay women less for equal work are better off: they faced no new damages exposure, class actions, or federal pay-data reporting, because the bill never received a vote.

for.name: 192 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 192 of 193 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican cosponsor [S4].

industries.note: The bill would make them liable for compensatory and punitive damages and class actions, and narrow the defenses they could raise, so their interest in defeating it ran directly against workers seeking equal pay [S3].
The bill would impose new reporting of pay and employment data by sex, race, and national origin and restrict wage-confidentiality clauses, even for employers with no pay gap [S2][S3].
